the real risk is if they stop getting contract-backed loans and have to borrow at that 15%.

say they need $20B more. at the ~6-9% they’ve been getting, that’s around $1.3-1.8B a year in interest. at 15% it’s $3B a year.

for context, they paid $640M in interest last quarter, so about $2.6B a year on everything they owe right now. one new $20B chunk at 15% would cost more than all of that. and they’re still not profitable.

the next financing deal is critical. if it’s contract-backed at single digits, fine. if they’re forced into 15% bonds, that’s when it gets really risky.

$CRWV isn’t paying 15% interest. Only 4% of their debt costs that.

I went through the Q2 10-Q line by line. Out of ~$35B in debt, exactly one loan sits at 15%. It’s $1.3B, due March 2028, and already being paid down.

The 15% chart going around is the market yield on their 2032 bond. A higher yield doesn’t change what CoreWeave pays. It works like a mortgage. If you locked in at 3% and rates go to 7%, you’re still paying 3%. CoreWeave locked that bond at 9.625% and still pays 9.625%.

What they actually pay

> $6.6B of convertibles at ~2%
> ~$10B of bonds at 9-10%
> Most secured loans around 9%
> ~8.4% blended across everything

They have roughly $20B of 2026 capex left to fund, and 2027 will need more. Their main funding tool has been loans backed by customer contracts. The investment grade one backed by Meta priced around 5.9% in March. If they keep borrowing that way, I think the math holds.

This is a great take on the current state of the AI trade.

On the equity side, tech trades at ~19x forward earnings. At the 2000 peak it was ~59x. Prices have run, but earnings have run faster, so the multiple is actually shrinking.

On the credit side, CoreWeave's implied yield went from ~9% to ~16%, tracing the same early path telecom junk bonds took before the dot-com bust.

The stress sits at the leveraged edge of the buildout. The bulk of it is paid for by hyperscalers with investment-grade balance sheets and enormous cash flows, and CoreWeave is about 4% of projected data center capacity.

If high-yield credit forces the weakest builders to slow down, the buildout gets slower and a lot more durable. 1999 never had that brake.

If CoreWeave's yield rolls over, the scare is behind us. If it heads into the 20s, well, we might have havoc on our hands…

Even then, CoreWeave is ~4% of projected data center capacity, and most of the other 96% sits on investment-grade balance sheets.

Contagion is real though, so stay vigilant.

The selloff continues. Next, I’m shifting from shorting beta to shorting alpha. I call it the “reverse bottleneck trade”—the counterpart to the earlier bottleneck trade.

The logic is simple: AI demand will keep growing, but that growth may slow, while upstream suppliers keep expanding capacity in response to shortages and fat margins. Once effective supply catches up with demand, bargaining power shifts back downstream. During a shortage, customers care first about availability. Good enough will do. Once supply is plentiful, they start comparing performance, cost, power consumption, and reliability again. That’s when we find out who wins orders on competitiveness and who was simply picking up overflow because the leaders couldn’t supply enough.

My watchlist includes memory runner-up MU, second- and third-tier optical players COHR and AAOI, and foundry runner-up INTC.

This trade doesn’t even require the AI bubble to burst. Supply growth just needs to start outpacing demand growth. I think there’s a very high probability these stocks put in an “Everest chart” over the next year—a towering peak followed by a collapse back down. If you don’t have the stomach to go all-in on outright shorts, anti-bottleneck pair trades are another good way to express the view: long LITE / short AAOI; long TSM / short INTC; long NVDA / short AMD or AVGO.

Here's the top 20 fastest-growing jobs from today until 2035:

1. Nurse practitioners (41%)
2. Solar photovoltaic installers (37%)
3. Data scientists (35%)
4. Wind turbine service technicians (30%)
5. Medical and health services managers (24%)
6. Physical therapist assistants (23%)
7. Psychiatric technicians (22%)
8. Computer and information research scientists (22%)
9. Occupational therapy assistants (21%)
10. Ophthalmic medical technicians (21%)
11. Physician assistants (21%)
12. Information security analysts (21%)
13. Occupational health and safety technicians (19%)
14. Hearing aid specialists (19%)
15. Epidemiologists (19%)
16. Occupational health and safety specialists (18%)
17. Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors (18%)
18. Home health and personal care aides (18%)
19. Health specialties teachers, postsecondary (18%)
20. Industrial machinery mechanics (18%)

What does this mean for the stock market?

Healthcare:
- healthcare is the largest category on this list. It is literally the future. Huge aging population
- the system also faces a binding capacity constraint. Physician shortages (especially primary care) are projected to persist deep into the 2030s
- home health aides, therapy assistants, and health services managers are scaling to support aging-in-place and higher-acuity outpatient care
- mental health and substance-use roles also reflect a multi-year crisis
- Stocks for advanced practice and managed care: $UNH, $ELV, $HUM, $CI 
- Stocks for devices: $ISRG, $SYK, $MDT, $BSX 
- Age-related: $LLY, $ABBV, $MRK, $AMGN, $NVO
- Senior housing: $WELL, $VTR 

Technology:
- data volume is compounding across every industry (including healthcare records, imaging, and claims)
- data scientists exist to turn that volume into usable signals
- AI requires continuous research, not just implementation.
- computer and information research scientists invent the next algorithms and systems as basic data science becomes more widespread
- connectivity permanently expands the attack surface - Information security analysts grow because the cost of being unsecured keeps rising; especially in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure
- stocks for AI infrastructure & platforms: $NVDA, $MSFT, $GOOGL, $AMZN, $AVGO, $AMD, $SNOW, $PLTR
- stocks for cybersecurity: $CRWD, $PANW, $ZS, $FTNT, $S, $OKTA

Renewables:
- solar and wind appear because of the energy transition, but the absolute job numbers remain small compared with healthcare and tech.
- solar photovoltaic installers and wind turbine technicians are high-percentage growth roles tied to new capacity and maintenance.
- these stocks remain more policy-sensitive and cyclical than the healthcare or cybersecurity names.
- stocks for renewables overall: $TSLA 
- stocks for solar: $ENPH, $SEDG, $FSLR, $RUN, $NOVA
- stocks for wind / clean energy: $GEV 

Industrials:
- industrial machinery mechanics is the main non-service name on the list.
- demand comes from keeping factories, production lines, and equipment running as manufacturing and automation continue.
- this is the more traditional industrial maintenance and equipment side of the economy.
- stocks: $SPCX, $CAT, $DE, $HON, $ETN, $ROK, $EMR

Okay so what to do?
In my opinion, healthcare is the biggest and most durable demand engine on this list. An aging population, doctor shortages, and the move toward more care at home and outside hospitals are already locked in. This is the part of the market that should act as the ballast in a portfolio. Have some real exposure to healthcare.

Tech (data, AI, and cybersecurity) is the higher-upside layer sitting on top of that. These names tend to move more when the market is in growth mode, but they also carry more volatility. So make sure you have exposure here in tech as well for the next decade to outperform the markets.  

Renewables and industrial machinery show up on the list, but they are smaller pieces of the overall picture and more sensitive to policy and the economic cycle. It's okay to have crazy volatile names, but make sure you size it correctly.

Whatever happens, let's continue to compound our winners and make millions together.

美股周三反复造好，科网股再成主导。标普500ETF（ $SPY ）收报773.09美元，升0.53%；纳指ETF（QQQ）升1.05%，收报725.20美元，为四大指数中表现一枝独秀；道指ETF（DIA）升0.64%，收报527.70美元；罗素小型股ETF（IWM）仅升0.25%，收报276.48美元，升幅约为纳指的四分之一，反映资金仍高度集中于大型科技及AI主线，未全面扩散至细价股。市宽亦印证此一格局：106只观察股中76只上升、30只下跌，升跌比约2.5比1，属偏好但并非一致普涨的升市。反向ETF全线急泻，沽空纳指的 SQQQ 挫3.18%，沽空半导体的 SOXS 暴跌6.03%，沽空标普的 SPXU 跌1.55%，其中芯片空头损伤最重，显示半导体日内升势最为凌厉。

**板块**
AI硬件及算力基建一线领升。SMCI 暴涨9.55%，居观察股升幅之首，DELL 升5.27%，服务器股同步造好；高速互连与光通信同获追捧，CRDO 升6.28%，CIEN 升5.67%。电力及能源设备方面，燃料电池股 BE 急升7.13%。软件与网络安全全线靠稳，MDB 升6.71%，NET 升5.32%，CRWD 升5.26%。航天股造好，RKLB 升5.41%。惟大型科技股内部分化明显，GOOGL 逆市跌1.64%，ORCL 跌1.53%，与AI硬件的凌厉升势形成对照。出行及旧经济股见沽压，UBER 跌1.91%，F 挫2.06%，广告科技股 APP 跌1.67%。中概股失守，BABA 重挫3.87%，跌幅在实质个股中仅次于 NFLX。

**焦点**
NFLX 为全日最大焦点。公司于前一交易日盘后公布业绩，今日正式反映，股价急泻5.31%，财报即为主因。另一只业绩股 SPCX 方向相反，同样于前一交易日盘后披露，今日大涨7.79%，高居升幅榜第二位。消息面上，市场流传 Meta 拟发行新股为AI基建融资，消息未经证实，现阶段仍属传闻；若最终成事，将首次扭转大型科技企业近十年"股数只往下走"的回购叙事，而换回的资产为折旧周期约六年的数据中心算力，惟公司未公布任何相关安排。能源方面，布伦特与WTI价差持续拉阔，分析指瓶颈在于美湾出口运力而非库欣库存，属运费问题多于供应问题。

**小结**
全日属"指数温和向上、板块高度集中"的格局：纳指ETF升幅数倍于小型股，升幅榜几乎由AI硬件与算力链独揽，而科技龙头、中概及旧经济同时承压。市宽76比30虽偏正面，但领升名单清一色集中于同一主线，升市基础并不宽阔。焦点将转向今晚盘后公布业绩的 META、TSLA、IBM、LRCX 及 TXN，其中芯片与半导体设备股的指引，将直接检验今日算力链升势的持续性；分析指，QQQ 能否守住725.20美元的收市水平，为短线观察的关键位。
